description: People with an interest in Space and the unknown!
summary:
CHRONO-OUTPOST: Rewrite the Mission is a browser game that teaches children aged 7–12 real space science by letting them rescue two NASA missions that went wrong: Apollo 13 (1970) and Mars Polar Lander (1999).

Players fly through a space storm, crash-land, and then keep a five-room habitat alive. Every day, an unexpected emergency strikes, built from real NASA DONKI space-weather records (solar flares, coronal mass ejections and particle storms) and NASA biology research. With only 10 power units to share, kids must make smart trade-offs, boosting one room by cutting another, to survive. Right choices advance the mission. Wrong choices show the consequences and explain the science behind them. After each decision, the game compares the player’s choice with real NASA history.

This matters because it turns passive facts into hands-on decisions. It teaches priorities, cause and effect, and real space science. It also shows children that, like NASA, we learn from failure.
details:
CHRONO-OUTPOST: Rewrite the Mission is a browser game for children aged 7–12. They travel back in time to two NASA missions that went wrong, Apollo 13 (1970) and Mars Polar Lander (1999), and try to save them.

1.Launch: Astro-Bot, a friendly astronaut riding a rocket, welcomes the player.

2.Choose a world: the Moon or Mars, with real facts about gravity, air and communication delay.

3.Briefing: the player reads the real history of the mission.

4.Cockpit storm: in a 15-second cockpit stage, the player dodges meteoroids or solar-flare plasma. The plasma is labelled with a real NASA DONKI flare. The engine then fails and the ship crash-lands. Flying well keeps the crew healthier later.

5.Habitat survival: the main game. The base has five rooms in priority order:

  • Life Support (air and heat)
  • Radiation Shield
  • Power
  • Space Garden
  • Science Lab

There are only 10 power units to share between them, so boosting one room means cutting another.

6.Daily emergencies: each day an alarm announces an unexpected event, such as an oxygen tank rupture, an X-class solar flare, a Martian dust storm, a −80 °C polar night or a hungry crew. The order is shuffled every game.

  • A correct trade-off plays a success animation and moves the mission forward.
  • A wrong trade-off shows the consequence and explains the science in simple words.
  • A “NASA Historical Log” then compares the player’s choice with what really happened.
  • “Ask Astro-Bot” gives hints, and “Inspect Real NASA Data” shows the exact NASA record behind each event.

7.Victory: reaching 100% Mission Progress unlocks a mission patch and a splashdown or lander-transmission animation.

Benefits:

  • Teaches resource trade-offs and priorities, a core engineering skill, through play instead of lectures.
  • Shows cause and effect: every decision has a visible result.
  • Introduces real space science: space weather, radiation, growing food in space, and life support.
  • Builds a healthy attitude to failure: mistakes are safe, explained, and lead to learning.

Accessible: runs in any web browser with no install, and works offline using a built-in archive of real NASA data, which suits classrooms with weak internet.

Intended impact:

We want to make NASA history and science hands-on for young learners, and spark interest in STEM careers. Teachers get a 10–15 minute classroom activity that combines history, science and decision-making. Kids leave knowing that NASA’s biggest successes came from learning from failures.

Tools, languages and software:

  • Languages: JavaScript (React/JSX), HTML and CSS.
  • Frameworks and libraries: React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Motion (animation), React Router, Axios, lucide-react icons, canvas-confetti.
  • Graphics and sound: every illustration (astronauts, mascot, planets, Earth, habitat, cockpit) is hand-built SVG and HTML5 Canvas. Every sound effect is generated in code with the Web Audio API, so the game contains no image or audio files.
  • Data: the NASA CCMC DONKI API (FLR, CME and SEP endpoints), live or from bundled real May 2024 storm records, plus NASA biology research facts and NASA mission history.
  • Other tools: Visual Studio Code, Git, Google Fonts, PptxGenJS for the slides, and Claude (Anthropic) as an AI coding assistant.
  • Hardware: standard laptops only. The game runs on any computer or tablet with a modern browser.

How is it creative?

  • Instead of teaching NASA history as a list of facts, kids rewrite famous failures as playable missions.
  • Real space-weather data becomes live game events, so a real solar flare from May 2024 becomes the emergency a child must solve.
  • The 10-unit power grid turns an abstract engineering idea (trade-offs) into a simple, tactile puzzle.
  • The animated habitat shows each choice happening: frost spreading, a forcefield deflecting flare rays, plants growing.
  • Every decision is paired with the real historical outcome.
  • Factors our team considered:
  • Age-appropriate design: simple language, big buttons, a friendly mascot, and help only when the child asks for it, so the game isn’t overwhelming.
  • Scientific honesty: neither real mission failed because of a solar storm. Space weather is our game’s challenge, and the in-game history panels always tell the true story. Game-only values are clearly labelled.
  • Real data with reliability: live NASA data when online, and an automatic fallback to real archived data when offline.
  • Learning through mistakes: players can always act, even wrongly, and every failure is explained.
  • Replay value: shuffled events and two different worlds.
  • Accessibility and reach: browser-based, no install, works on school devices.
  • Responsible use: no NASA logos or insignia, AI use disclosed, and AI-made visuals labelled.
